nodes.name: Bernstein block
nodes.statement: In \cite{Bernstein1984}, J.~Bernstein gives a decomposition of the category of smooth representations of $G$ into indecomposable full subcategories, called \emph{blocks}, that are indexed by the inertial support of the irreducible representations they contain.
nodes.statement_short: A block is an indecomposable full subcategory of smooth representations of $G$, indexed by inertial support.

nodes.name: type for a supercuspidal representation
nodes.statement: Given an irreducible supercuspidal representation $\pi$ of $G$, a \emph{type} for $\pi$ is a pair $(K, \lambda)$ consisting of an irreducible representation $\lambda$ of a compact open subgroup $K$ of $G$ such that $\Ind_K^G \lambda$ is a projective generator of the block containing $\pi$. In this case, $\lambda$ occurs as a subrepresentation of $\pi|_K$ and we say $\pi$ \emph{contains} the type $(K,\lambda)$.
nodes.statement_short: A type for $\pi$ is a compact-open pair $(K,\lambda)$ whose induction generates the Bernstein block of $\pi$.
nodes.genus: a pair $(K, \lambda)$ consisting of an irreducible representation $\lambda$ of a compact open subgroup $K$ of $G$
differentia: $\Ind_K^G \lambda$ is a projective generator of the block containing $\pi$

nodes.name: Existence of types for essentially tame supercuspidal representations (Adler-Yu)
nodes.statement: In particular, the work of J.~Adler \cite{Adler1998}, generalized by J.K.~Yu \cite{Yu2001}, shows that every essentially tame supercuspidal representation contains a type;
nodes.statement_short: Every essentially tame supercuspidal representation contains a type (Adler, generalized by Yu).
conclusions: every essentially tame supercuspidal representation contains a type

nodes.name: Kim's exhaustion theorem
nodes.statement: the work of J.-L.~Kim \cite{Kim2007} assures us that if the residual characteristic $p$ is sufficiently large, then all supercuspidal representations of $G$ are of this form.
nodes.statement_short: For large residual characteristic, every supercuspidal representation of $G$ is essentially tame.
assumptions: if the residual characteristic $p$ is sufficiently large
conclusions: all supercuspidal representations of $G$ are of this form

nodes.name: Production of additional types from a given type
nodes.statement: Given a supercuspidal representation $\pi$ of $G$ containing a type $(K,\lambda)$, it is simple to produce additional types: any $G$-conjugate of $(K,\lambda)$ is a type, as is any pair $(K', \tau)$ where $K'$ is a compact open subgroup of $G$ containing $K$ and $\tau$ is an irreducible representation of $K'$ that contains $\lambda$ upon restriction to $K$.
nodes.statement_short: Conjugates of a type, and representations of larger compact opens containing it, are again types.
assumptions: Given a supercuspidal representation $\pi$ of $G$ containing a type $(K,\lambda)$
conclusions: any $G$-conjugate of $(K,\lambda)$ is a type, as is any pair $(K', \tau)$ where $K'$ is a compact open subgroup of $G$ containing $K$ and $\tau$ is an irreducible representation of $K'$ that contains $\lambda$ upon restriction to $K$

nodes.name: Unicity of types
nodes.statement: A natural question to ask is whether $\pi$ can contain any additional types, specifically on \emph{maximal} compact open subgroups, that are not related to $(K,\lambda)$ in this way. It is expected that this should never happen, and the conjecture that this is the case is known as the \emph{unicity of types}.
nodes.statement_short: Conjecturally, all types of $\pi$ on maximal compact open subgroups arise from a single one by conjugation and induction.
conclusions: It is expected that this should never happen, and the conjecture that this is the case is known as the \emph{unicity of types}

nodes.name: Known cases of the unicity conjecture
nodes.statement: The unicity conjecture is a theorem for $G=\GL_n(\ratk)$ \cite{Paskunas2005}, $G=\SL_2(\ratk)$ \cite{Latham2016}, for essentially tame representations of $G=\SL_n(\ratk)$ \cite{Latham2018}, and for depth-zero supercuspidal representations of any connected reductive $p$-adic group $G$ \cite{Latham2017}.
nodes.statement_short: Unicity is known for $\GL_n$, $\SL_2$, essentially tame representations of $\SL_n$, and depth-zero supercuspidals.
conclusions: The unicity conjecture is a theorem for $G=\GL_n(\ratk)$ \cite{Paskunas2005}, $G=\SL_2(\ratk)$ \cite{Latham2016}, for essentially tame representations of $G=\SL_n(\ratk)$ \cite{Latham2018}, and for depth-zero supercuspidal representations of any connected reductive $p$-adic group $G$ \cite{Latham2017}

nodes.name: strong unicity property
nodes.statement: In each of these cases, it was seen that a stronger property holds, namely, that if $K\subset G$ is any maximal compact open subgroup, then there exists, up to $G$-conjugacy, at most one type defined on $K$ for each supercuspidal representation $\pi$ of $G$. We will refer to this as the \emph{strong unicity property}.
nodes.statement_short: Strong unicity: each maximal compact open subgroup carries at most one type per supercuspidal, up to $G$-conjugacy.

nodes.name: toral supercuspidal representation
nodes.statement: We restrict our attention here to those sequences for which the smallest twisted Levi subgroup is an anisotropic (also called elliptic) maximal torus of $G$. For the purposes of this paper we call these \emph{toral} supercuspidal representations, though we caution the reader that some authors reserve ``toral'' to mean the more restrictive case that the twisted Levi sequence has length $d=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Toral (= positive regular) supercuspidals are those whose smallest twisted Levi subgroup is an anisotropic maximal torus.

nodes.name: Strategy for proving the unicity conjecture
nodes.statement: The strategy for proving the unicity conjecture for supercuspidal representations of $G$ is as follows. Let $\pi$ be an essentially tame supercuspidal representation and $(\KT,\kappa)$ a type as arising from the above construction. Since $G$ is semisimple and simply connected, we have both that $\cind_{\KT}^G\kappa$ is irreducible (hence equivalent to $\pi$) and that every maximal compact open subgroup of $G$ is the stabilizer $G_y$ of a vertex $y$ in the Bruhat-Tits building of $G$. Thus for any such $G_y$ containing $\KT$, it follows directly that we have an induced type $(G_y,\Ind_{\KT}^{G_y}\kappa)$.
nodes.statement_short: For $G$ semisimple simply connected, every maximal compact is a vertex stabilizer $G_y$, and each $G_y\supseteq\KT$ carries an induced type.

nodes.name: Reformulation of unicity and strong unicity
nodes.statement: The conjecture of unicity of types therefore amounts to the statement that, up to $G$-conjugacy, all types for $\pi$ on a maximal compact open subgroup arise in this way. Strong unicity is the statement that furthermore any two types for $\pi$ on $G_y$ are conjugate by an element of $N_G(G_y)$; this is equivalent to the statement that $(\KT,\kappa)$ is not contained two distinct but conjugate maximal compact open subgroups.
nodes.statement_short: Unicity says all types on maximal compacts are induced from $(\KT,\kappa)$; strong unicity says any two on $G_y$ are $N_G(G_y)$-conjugate.

nodes.name: Branching rules for the restriction of $\pi$ to a maximal compact open subgroup
nodes.statement: The restriction of $\pi$ to a maximal compact open subgroup $G_y$ decomposes as an infinite direct sum of irreducible representations of $G_y$. Describing these branching rules is a difficult open problem of interest in its own right.
nodes.statement_short: Describing the decomposition of $\pi|_{G_y}$ into irreducibles is an open problem.

nodes.name: Main Theorem (unicity for toral supercuspidal representations)
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a tame elliptic maximal torus of $G$ and suppose $\pi$ is a supercuspidal representation of $G$ built from a datum containing $T$. If the character $\phi_0$ of $T$ appearing in the datum has depth greater than $2c_T$, then $\pi$ satisfies the unicity conjecture relative to any maximal compact open subgroup of $G$. Moreover, in this case, $\pi$ satisfies the strong unicity property if and only if $\buil^T$ consists precisely of the closure of a single facet in $\buil(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: If $\phi_0$ has depth $>2c_T$ then $\pi$ satisfies unicity, and strong unicity exactly when $\buil^T$ is the closure of one facet.
assumptions: Let $T$ be a tame elliptic maximal torus of $G$
$\pi$ is a supercuspidal representation of $G$ built from a datum containing $T$
If the character $\phi_0$ of $T$ appearing in the datum has depth greater than $2c_T$
conclusions: then $\pi$ satisfies the unicity conjecture relative to any maximal compact open subgroup of $G$
Moreover, in this case, $\pi$ satisfies the strong unicity property if and only if $\buil^T$ consists precisely of the closure of a single facet in $\buil(G)$

nodes.name: Remaining open problems on unicity of types
nodes.statement: Several interesting problems remain open. The hypothesis on the depth of the character of $T$ given in the statement of Theorem~\ref{T:unicity} arises as a result of our method of proof. There is no such restriction for the unicity theorems on $G=\GL_n$ or on $G=\SL_n$, where a different argument (particular to type A) was employed by V.~Pa\u{s}k\={u}nas to address the small-depth case. Finally, not all essentially tame supercuspidal representations arise from toral data; the consideration of general twisted Levi sequences is necessary to completely resolve the unicity conjecture in these cases.
nodes.statement_short: Removing the depth hypothesis, and handling general (non-toral) twisted Levi sequences, remain open.

nodes.name: twisted Levi subgroup
nodes.statement: We say that a group $\GG'$ (or its set of $\ratk$-points $G' = \GG'(\ratk)$) is a \emph{twisted Levi subgroup} of $\GG$ if there is an extension $\extk$ of $\ratk$ such that $\GG'$ is an $\extk$-Levi subgroup of $\GG$ defined over $\ratk$. We say $\GG'$ is tamely ramified if $\GG'$ (and thus $\GG$) splits over a tamely ramified extension.
nodes.statement_short: A twisted Levi subgroup becomes a Levi subgroup after base change to some extension field; it is tamely ramified if it splits tamely.
differentia: there is an extension $\extk$ of $\ratk$ such that $\GG'$ is an $\extk$-Levi subgroup of $\GG$ defined over $\ratk$

nodes.name: Moy-Prasad filtration subgroups
nodes.statement: For any $x\in \apart$ and $r\geq 0$, A.~Moy and G.~Prasad \cite{MoyPrasad1994} defined $G_{\alpha,x,r} = \langle G_\psi \mid \psi(x)\geq r, \dot\psi=\alpha \rangle$ and thus filtration subgroups $$ G_{x,r}=\langle Z_{r}, G_{\alpha,x,r} \mid \alpha \in \Phi\rangle $$ of $G_x$. We set $G_{x,r+} = \cup_{s>r}G_{x,s}$. They similarly defined lattices $\LieG_{x,r}$ in $\LieG=\Lie(G)(\ratk)$ and $\LieG^*_{x,r}$ in $\LieG^*$, indexed by $r\in \mathbb{R}$. Conjugation by $G$ allows us to extend these definitions to any $x\in \buil(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: $G_{x,r}$ is generated by $Z_r$ and the affine root groups $G_{\alpha,x,r}$; the same recipe filters $\LieG$ and $\LieG^*$.

nodes.name: $G$-generic element of depth $-r$
nodes.statement: Following \cite[Definition 3.7]{HakimMurnaghan2008}, an element $X^* \in {\mz'}^*_{-r}$ is called \emph{$G$-generic of depth $-r$} if it satisfies the conditions \textbf{GE1} and \textbf{GE2} of \cite[\S8]{Yu2001}.
differentia: it satisfies the conditions \textbf{GE1} and \textbf{GE2} of \cite[\S8]{Yu2001}

nodes.name: Reduction of the genericity conditions GE1 and GE2
nodes.statement: By \cite[Lemma 8.1]{Yu2001}, if $p$ is not a torsion prime for the root datum (in the sense of \cite{Springer1977}) of $(\GG,\TT)$, then these conditions reduce to the requirement that $\nu(\langle X^*, H_a\rangle) = -r$, for each $a \in \Phi(\GG,\TT)\setminus\Phi(\GG',\TT)$, where $H_a \in \Lie(\GG)(\extk)$ is the coroot associated to $a$.
nodes.statement_short: Away from torsion primes, $G$-genericity of $X^*$ is just a valuation condition on its pairings with coroots.
assumptions: if $p$ is not a torsion prime for the root datum (in the sense of \cite{Springer1977}) of $(\GG,\TT)$
conclusions: these conditions reduce to the requirement that $\nu(\langle X^*, H_a\rangle) = -r$, for each $a \in \Phi(\GG,\TT)\setminus\Phi(\GG',\TT)$, where $H_a \in \Lie(\GG)(\extk)$ is the coroot associated to $a$

nodes.name: Moy-Prasad isomorphism
nodes.statement: Fix also a Moy-Prasad isomorphism \cite[\S 2.6]{HakimMurnaghan2008} $$ e \colon G'_{x,r}/G'_{x,r+} \to \LieG'_{x,r}/\LieG'_{x,r+}. $$

nodes.name: character realized by an element $X^*$ on $G'_{x,r}$
nodes.statement: A character $\phi$ of $G'$ of depth $r$ is said to be \emph{realized by an element $X^* \in {\mz'}^{*}_{-r}$ on $G'_{x,r}$} if for every $Y \in \LieG'_{x,r}$, $$ \phi(e(Y+\LieG'_{x,r+})) = \Lambda(\langle X^*, Y\rangle). $$
nodes.statement_short: $\phi$ is realized by $X^*$ when it is the pullback of $\Lambda\langle X^*,\cdot\rangle$ under the Moy-Prasad isomorphism.

nodes.name: $G$-generic character of depth $r$
nodes.statement: By \cite[Definition 3.9]{HakimMurnaghan2008}, $\phi$ is \emph{$G$-generic (relative to $x$) of depth $r>0$} if $\phi$ is trivial on $G'_{x,r+}$, nontrivial on $G'_{x,r}$, and is realized on $G'_{x,r}$ by an element $X^* \in {\mz'}^{*}_{-r}$ that is $G$-generic of depth $-r$.
nodes.statement_short: A character is $G$-generic of depth $r$ if it is trivial on $G'_{x,r+}$, nontrivial on $G'_{x,r}$, and realized by a $G$-generic $X^*$.
differentia: is realized on $G'_{x,r}$ by an element $X^* \in {\mz'}^{*}_{-r}$ that is $G$-generic of depth $-r$

nodes.name: Genericity detects the twisted Levi subgroup
nodes.statement: A particular consequence of the $G$-genericity of a character $\phi$ of $G'$ is that for any $g\in G$, we have that ${}^g\phi$ and $\phi$ coincide on $G'_{x,r}$ if and only if $g\in G'$ \cite[Lemma 8.3]{Yu2001}.
nodes.statement_short: For a $G$-generic $\phi$, ${}^g\phi=\phi$ on $G'_{x,r}$ forces $g\in G'$.
assumptions: for any $g\in G$
conclusions: we have that ${}^g\phi$ and $\phi$ coincide on $G'_{x,r}$ if and only if $g\in G'$

nodes.name: positive-depth generic toral supercuspidal datum of length $d$
nodes.statement: Following \cite[\S3]{Yu2001} and \cite[\S3.1]{HakimMurnaghan2008}, we define a \emph{positive-depth generic toral supercuspidal datum of length $d$} of $G$ (hereafter: \emph{toral supercuspidal datum}) to be a pair $(\vec{G}, \vec{\phi})$, where \begin{itemize} \item $\vec{G} = (G^0\subsetneq G^1 \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq G^d=G)$, for some $d \geq 1$, is a sequence of tamely ramified twisted Levi subgroups, such that in particular $G^0=T$ an anisotropic maximal torus in $G$; \item $\vec{\phi} = (\phi_0, \phi_1, \ldots, \phi_{d-1})$ where $\phi_i$ is a $G^{i+1}$-generic character of $G^i$ of depth $r_i$, and these real numbers satisfy $0<r_0<r_1 < \cdots < r_{d-1}$. \end{itemize} For convenience we write $s_i = r_i/2$ for each $i = 0, \ldots, d-1$.
nodes.statement_short: A toral datum is a tower of tamely ramified twisted Levi subgroups starting at an anisotropic maximal torus, together with generic characters of increasing depth.

nodes.name: the point $x$ attached to a toral datum
nodes.statement: Given a tamely ramified twisted Levi subgroup $\GG'$ of $\GG$ that is defined over $\ratk$, one may embed $\buil(\GG',\ratk)$ into $\buil(\GG,\ratk)$ with canonical image. Since $T$ is anisotropic, the image of $\buil(T)$ in $\buil(G)$ consists of a single point $x$, and it is this point relative to which the characters $\phi_i$ are $G^{i+1}$-generic. Thus a toral supercuspidal datum implies the datum $(\vec{G}, \vec{\phi}, d, \vec{r}, \vec{s}, x)$, and we will take this extra data for granted where there is no possibility of confusion.
nodes.statement_short: Anisotropy of $T$ makes $\buil(T)$ a single point $x$ of $\buil(G)$, relative to which all $\phi_i$ are generic.

nodes.name: the groups $\KT^i$
nodes.statement: Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ be a toral supercuspidal datum. Set $\KT^0=G^0_x=T$. For each $1\leq i\leq d$ define $$ \KT^i:= G^0_{x}G^1_{x,s_0}\cdots G^{i}_{x,s_{i-1}} \subseteq TG_{x,s_0} \subseteq G_x. $$
nodes.statement_short: $\KT^i$ is the product of $T$ with the Moy-Prasad subgroups $G^j_{x,s_{j-1}}$ up to level $i$.

nodes.name: the groups $\J^{i+1}$ and $\J^{i+1}_+$
nodes.statement: The groups in these products have large pairwise intersections, so we next define subgroups $\J^i$ and $\J^i_+$ which will have the property that $\KT^i\J^{i+1}=\KT^{i+1}$ and $\KT^i\cap \J^{i+1} = \KT^i\cap \J^{i+1}_+ = G^i_{x,r_i}$. Let $\extk$ be a tamely ramified Galois extension of $\ratk$ over which $\TT$ splits. For each $0\leq i\leq d$, let $\Phi_i = \Phi(\GG^i,\TT)$ be the corresponding root system. For $0 \leq i < d$ let $\J(\extk)^{i+1}$ be the group generated by $\TT(\extk)_{r_{i}}$ together with the root subgroups $\GG_a(\extk)_{x,r_{i}}$ for $a\in \Phi_{i}$ and $\GG_b(\extk)_{x,s_{i}}$ for $b\in \Phi_{i+1}\setminus \Phi_{i}$. Similarly, let $$ \J(\extk)^{i+1}_+ = \langle \TT(\extk)_{r_{i}}, \GG_a(\extk)_{x,r_{i}}, \GG_b(\extk)_{x,s_{i}+} \mid a\in \Phi_{i}, b\in \Phi_{i+1}\setminus \Phi_{i} \rangle. $$ These subgroups of $\GG^{i+1}(\extk)$ are invariant under $\Gal(\extk/\ratk)$ and we set $\J^{i+1}=\J(E)^{i+1}\cap G^{i+1}$, $\J^{i+1}_+ = \J(\extk)^{i+1}_+\cap G^{i+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\J^{i+1},\J^{i+1}_+$ are Galois-fixed points of root-group products over $\extk$, chosen so that $\KT^i\J^{i+1}=\KT^{i+1}$.

nodes.name: Adler-Yu construction of the type $(\KT,\kappa(\Psi))$
nodes.statement: Next for each $0\leq i <d$, the subdatum $((G^i,G^{i+1}), \phi_i)$ is used to construct a representation $\phi_i'$ of $\KT^{i+1}$. The first step is to extend the restriction of $\phi_i$ to $G^i_{x,r_i}$ trivially to a character $\hat\phi_i$ of $J^{i+1}_+$ \cite[\S4]{Yu2001}. Next, when $\J^{i+1}_+=\J^{i+1}$, define a character $\phi_i'$ of $\KT^{i+1}$ by \begin{equation} \phi_i'(kj)=\phi_i(k)\hat\phi_i(j), \end{equation} for each $k\in \KT^i$, $j\in \J^{i+1}$. On the other hand, when $\J^{i+1}_+ \neq \J^{i+1}$, then instead one uses $\hat\phi_i$ to construct a Heisenberg-Weil representation $\omega$ of $\KT^i\ltimes \J^{i+1}$, and then define the representation $\phi_i'$ on $k\in \KT^i$, $j\in \J^{i+1}$ by \begin{equation} \phi_i'(kj) = \phi_i(k)\omega(k,j). \end{equation} Now set $\KT = \KT^d$. There is a well-defined inflation process extending each $\phi_i'$ trivially across the remaining subgroups to give a representation of $\KT$, which we denote $\kappa_i=\inf_{\KT^{i+1}}^{\KT}\phi_i'$ \cite[\S3.4]{HakimMurnaghan2008}. Note that this representation $\kappa_i$ is independent of any other characters $\phi_j$, $j\neq i$, in the datum \cite[Proposition 3.26]{HakimMurnaghan2008}. Putting these together, we obtain a representation $\kappa(\Psi)= \kappa_{0}\otimes \cdots \otimes \kappa_{d-1}$ of $\KT$ such that $\pi (\Psi) = \cind_{\KT}^G \kappa(\Psi)$ is an irreducible supercuspidal representation of $G$ of depth $r=r_{d-1}$ \cite[Theorem 15.1]{Yu2001}. It then follows that $(\KT,\kappa(\Psi))$ is a type for $\pi(\Psi)$.
nodes.statement_short: From a toral datum, build $\phi_i'$ on $\KT^{i+1}$ (Heisenberg-Weil twisted when $\J^{i+1}_+\neq\J^{i+1}$), inflate to $\kappa_i$, tensor, and compactly induce to get $\pi(\Psi)$.

nodes.name: Define $\phi_i'$ when $\J^{i+1}_+=\J^{i+1}$
nodes.statement: Next, when $\J^{i+1}_+=\J^{i+1}$, define a character $\phi_i'$ of $\KT^{i+1}$ by \begin{equation} \phi_i'(kj)=\phi_i(k)\hat\phi_i(j), \end{equation} for each $k\in \KT^i$, $j\in \J^{i+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: In the degenerate case set $\phi_i'(kj)=\phi_i(k)\hat\phi_i(j)$.

nodes.name: Define $\phi_i'$ via a Heisenberg-Weil representation
nodes.statement: On the other hand, when $\J^{i+1}_+ \neq \J^{i+1}$, then instead one uses $\hat\phi_i$ to construct a Heisenberg-Weil representation $\omega$ of $\KT^i\ltimes \J^{i+1}$, and then define the representation $\phi_i'$ on $k\in \KT^i$, $j\in \J^{i+1}$ by \begin{equation} \phi_i'(kj) = \phi_i(k)\omega(k,j). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise twist by the Heisenberg-Weil representation $\omega$ of $\KT^i\ltimes\J^{i+1}$.

nodes.name: Inflate $\phi_i'$ to $\kappa_i$ on $\KT$
nodes.statement: Now set $\KT = \KT^d$. There is a well-defined inflation process extending each $\phi_i'$ trivially across the remaining subgroups to give a representation of $\KT$, which we denote $\kappa_i=\inf_{\KT^{i+1}}^{\KT}\phi_i'$ \cite[\S3.4]{HakimMurnaghan2008}.
nodes.statement_short: Inflate each $\phi_i'$ trivially across the remaining subgroups to a representation $\kappa_i$ of $\KT$.

nodes.name: Tensor and compactly induce
nodes.statement: Putting these together, we obtain a representation $\kappa(\Psi)= \kappa_{0}\otimes \cdots \otimes \kappa_{d-1}$ of $\KT$ such that $\pi (\Psi) = \cind_{\KT}^G \kappa(\Psi)$ is an irreducible supercuspidal representation of $G$ of depth $r=r_{d-1}$ \cite[Theorem 15.1]{Yu2001}. It then follows that $(\KT,\kappa(\Psi))$ is a type for $\pi(\Psi)$.
nodes.statement_short: Set $\kappa(\Psi)=\bigotimes_i\kappa_i$ and return $\pi(\Psi)=\cind_{\KT}^G\kappa(\Psi)$, a type-carrying supercuspidal.

nodes.statement: Note that this representation $\kappa_i$ is independent of any other characters $\phi_j$, $j\neq i$, in the datum \cite[Proposition 3.26]{HakimMurnaghan2008}.

nodes.statement_short: Compact induction of $\kappa(\Psi)$ from $\KT$ is an irreducible supercuspidal representation of depth $r_{d-1}$.

conclusions: $\pi (\Psi) = \cind_{\KT}^G \kappa(\Psi)$ is an irreducible supercuspidal representation of $G$ of depth $r=r_{d-1}$

nodes.name: Hakim-Murnaghan
nodes.statement: Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ and $\dot\Psi = (\vec{\dot{G}}, \vec{\dot{\phi}})$ be two toral supercuspidal data. Then $\pi(\Psi) \cong \pi(\dot\Psi)$ if and only if there exists some $g\in G$ such that $G^0 = {}^g\dot{G}^0$ and $\Res_{G^0}(\phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})=\Res_{G^0}{}^g(\dot{\phi}_0 \dot{\phi}_1 \cdots \dot{\phi}_{d-1})$. In this case, $G^i={}^g\dot{G}^i$ for all $i\geq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Two toral data give equivalent representations exactly when a single $g\in G$ matches their tori and the products of their characters.
assumptions: Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ and $\dot\Psi = (\vec{\dot{G}}, \vec{\dot{\phi}})$ be two toral supercuspidal data
conclusions: Then $\pi(\Psi) \cong \pi(\dot\Psi)$ if and only if there exists some $g\in G$ such that $G^0 = {}^g\dot{G}^0$ and $\Res_{G^0}(\phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})=\Res_{G^0}{}^g(\dot{\phi}_0 \dot{\phi}_1 \cdots \dot{\phi}_{d-1})$
In this case, $G^i={}^g\dot{G}^i$ for all $i\geq 0$

nodes.name: the twisted datum $\Psi_\xi$
nodes.statement: Now suppose $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ is a toral supercuspidal datum of length $d$ with $T=G^0$. Let $\xi$ be a character of $T$ of depth strictly less than $r_0$. The $G^1$-genericity of the character $\phi_0$ of $G^0$ of depth $r_0$ depends only on $\Res_{G^0_{x,r_0}}\phi$. Since $\xi\phi_0$ and $\phi_0$ coincide on $G^0_{x,r_0}$, we conclude that $\xi\phi_0$ is also a $G^1$-generic character of $G^0$ of depth $r_0$. Thus $$ \Psi_\xi = (\vec{G}, (\xi\phi_0, \phi_1,\ldots, \phi_{d-1})) $$ is another toral supercuspidal datum.
nodes.statement_short: Twisting $\phi_0$ by a character $\xi$ of $T$ of depth $<r_0$ again yields a toral supercuspidal datum $\Psi_\xi$.

nodes.name: Inflation of the twist
nodes.statement: The character $\xi$ inflates to a character $\overline{\xi}$ of $\KT$ such that $$ \kappa(\Psi_\xi) = \overline{\xi}\;\kappa(\Psi). $$
nodes.statement_short: The twist $\xi$ inflates to $\overline{\xi}$ on $\KT$ and factors out: $\kappa(\Psi_\xi)=\overline{\xi}\kappa(\Psi)$.
assumptions: Let $\xi$ be a character of $T$ of depth strictly less than $r_0$.
conclusions: The character $\xi$ inflates to a character $\overline{\xi}$ of $\KT$ such that $$ \kappa(\Psi_\xi) = \overline{\xi}\;\kappa(\Psi). $$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (inflation of the twist)
nodes.statement: Since $\xi$ is a character of $T=G^0=\KT^0$ of depth less than $r_0$, it is trivial on $G^0_{x,r_0}$. Since $\KT^1=\KT^0\J^1$ and $\KT^0\cap \J^1 = G^0_{x,r_0}$, $\xi$ may be uniquely inflated to a character $\xi' = \inf_{\KT^0}^{\KT^1}\xi$ of $\KT^1$ that is trivial on $\J^1$. In particular, for any $k\in \KT^0$, $j\in \J^{1}$, we have $\xi'(kj)=\xi(k)$. Since $\phi_0$ and $\xi\phi_0$ coincide on $G^0_{x,r_0}$, we may denote the extension to $\J^1_+$ of their common restriction by $\hat\phi_0$ and, if applicable, the corresponding Heisenberg-Weil representation of $\KT^0 \ltimes \J^1$ by $\omega$. Using now \eqref{E:phi'1} and \eqref{E:phi'2}, as applicable, to construct $(\xi\phi_0)'$ and $\phi_0'$, we deduce that in both cases $(\xi\phi_0)' = \xi' \phi_0'$. Set $\overline{\xi} = \inf_{\KT^1}^{\KT}\xi'$; then $\inf_{\KT^1}^{\KT}\xi'\phi_0' = \overline{\xi}\kappa_0$. Since for $i>0$, $\kappa_i$ depends only on the character $\phi_i$, we conclude that $\overline{\xi}$ factors out of the tensor product to yield $ \kappa(\Psi_\xi) = \overline{\xi}\kappa(\Psi), $ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Inflate $\xi$ to $\KT^1$ using $\KT^0\cap\J^1=G^0_{x,r_0}$, check $(\xi\phi_0)'=\xi'\phi_0'$ in both construction cases, then inflate to $\KT$.

nodes.name: Inflate $\xi$ to $\KT^1$
nodes.statement: Since $\xi$ is a character of $T=G^0=\KT^0$ of depth less than $r_0$, it is trivial on $G^0_{x,r_0}$. Since $\KT^1=\KT^0\J^1$ and $\KT^0\cap \J^1 = G^0_{x,r_0}$, $\xi$ may be uniquely inflated to a character $\xi' = \inf_{\KT^0}^{\KT^1}\xi$ of $\KT^1$ that is trivial on $\J^1$. In particular, for any $k\in \KT^0$, $j\in \J^{1}$, we have $\xi'(kj)=\xi(k)$.
nodes.statement_short: Triviality on $G^0_{x,r_0}$ lets $\xi$ inflate uniquely to $\xi'$ on $\KT^1$, trivial on $\J^1$.

nodes.name: Identify $(\xi\phi_0)' = \xi'\phi_0'$
nodes.statement: Since $\phi_0$ and $\xi\phi_0$ coincide on $G^0_{x,r_0}$, we may denote the extension to $\J^1_+$ of their common restriction by $\hat\phi_0$ and, if applicable, the corresponding Heisenberg-Weil representation of $\KT^0 \ltimes \J^1$ by $\omega$. Using now \eqref{E:phi'1} and \eqref{E:phi'2}, as applicable, to construct $(\xi\phi_0)'$ and $\phi_0'$, we deduce that in both cases $(\xi\phi_0)' = \xi' \phi_0'$.
nodes.statement_short: Both construction formulas give $(\xi\phi_0)'=\xi'\phi_0'$ since $\hat\phi_0$ and $\omega$ are unchanged by the twist.

nodes.name: Inflate to $\KT$ and factor out of the tensor product
nodes.statement: Set $\overline{\xi} = \inf_{\KT^1}^{\KT}\xi'$; then $\inf_{\KT^1}^{\KT}\xi'\phi_0' = \overline{\xi}\kappa_0$. Since for $i>0$, $\kappa_i$ depends only on the character $\phi_i$, we conclude that $\overline{\xi}$ factors out of the tensor product to yield $ \kappa(\Psi_\xi) = \overline{\xi}\kappa(\Psi), $ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Inflating to $\KT$ and using that $\kappa_i$ depends only on $\phi_i$, $\overline{\xi}$ factors out.

nodes.name: Inequivalence of twisted toral supercuspidal representations
nodes.statement: Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ be a toral supercuspidal datum and suppose $\xi$ is a character of $T=G^0$ of depth less than that of $\phi_0$. If $\Psi_\xi = (\vec{G}, (\xi\phi_0, \phi_1,\ldots,\phi_{d-1}))$, then $\pi(\Psi_\xi)$ is an irreducible supercuspidal representation of $G$ and it is equivalent to $\pi(\Psi)$ if and only if $\xi$ is trivial.
nodes.statement_short: A low-depth twist $\xi$ of $\phi_0$ changes the representation unless $\xi$ is trivial.
assumptions: Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ be a toral supercuspidal datum
suppose $\xi$ is a character of $T=G^0$ of depth less than that of $\phi_0$
If $\Psi_\xi = (\vec{G}, (\xi\phi_0, \phi_1,\ldots,\phi_{d-1}))$
conclusions: then $\pi(\Psi_\xi)$ is an irreducible supercuspidal representation of $G$ and it is equivalent to $\pi(\Psi)$ if and only if $\xi$ is trivial

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition (inequivalence of twists)
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\pi(\Psi) \cong \pi(\Psi_\xi)$. In the setting of Lemma~\ref{HMCor}, this means there is some $g \in N_G(T)$ such that $\Res_{T}(\phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})=\Res_{T}{}^g(\xi \phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})$. Then ${}^g(\xi\phi_0){}^g\phi_1\cdots {}^g \phi_{d-1}$ is a refactorization of $\phi_0\cdots \phi_{d-1}$, in the sense of \cite[Definition 5.3]{Murnaghan2011}, and so by \cite[Proposition 5.4]{Murnaghan2011}, for each $i>0$, $\prod_{j=i}^d \phi_j$ and $\prod_{j=i}^d {}^g\phi_j$ coincide on $G^i_{x,r_{i-1}+}$. The genericity of the characters $\phi_j$ recursively implies, as in the proof of \cite[Proposition 5.6]{Murnaghan2011}, that $g\in G^1$, and so ${}^g\phi_i=\phi_i$ for all $i\geq 1$. Therefore our equality reduces to $\Res_{T_{r_0}} \phi_0 = \Res_{T_{r_0}} {}^g(\xi\phi_0) = \Res_{T_{r_0}} {}^g\phi_0$, whence $g\in T$ by genericity. Returning to the first equality we conclude that $\xi$ is the trivial character of $T$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume equivalence, apply Hakim-Murnaghan and Murnaghan's refactorization results to force $g\in T$, hence $\xi$ trivial.

nodes.name: Apply the Hakim-Murnaghan equivalence criterion
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\pi(\Psi) \cong \pi(\Psi_\xi)$. In the setting of Lemma~\ref{HMCor}, this means there is some $g \in N_G(T)$ such that $\Res_{T}(\phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})=\Res_{T}{}^g(\xi \phi_0 \phi_1 \cdots \phi_{d-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Equivalence yields $g\in N_G(T)$ matching the restricted character products.

nodes.name: Recognize a refactorization
nodes.statement: Then ${}^g(\xi\phi_0){}^g\phi_1\cdots {}^g \phi_{d-1}$ is a refactorization of $\phi_0\cdots \phi_{d-1}$, in the sense of \cite[Definition 5.3]{Murnaghan2011}, and so by \cite[Proposition 5.4]{Murnaghan2011}, for each $i>0$, $\prod_{j=i}^d \phi_j$ and $\prod_{j=i}^d {}^g\phi_j$ coincide on $G^i_{x,r_{i-1}+}$.
nodes.statement_short: The twisted product is a refactorization, so partial products agree on $G^i_{x,r_{i-1}+}$.

nodes.name: Use genericity to place $g$ in $G^1$
nodes.statement: The genericity of the characters $\phi_j$ recursively implies, as in the proof of \cite[Proposition 5.6]{Murnaghan2011}, that $g\in G^1$, and so ${}^g\phi_i=\phi_i$ for all $i\geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Recursive genericity forces $g\in G^1$ and fixes all $\phi_i$, $i\geq1$.

nodes.name: Conclude $\xi$ is trivial
nodes.statement: Therefore our equality reduces to $\Res_{T_{r_0}} \phi_0 = \Res_{T_{r_0}} {}^g(\xi\phi_0) = \Res_{T_{r_0}} {}^g\phi_0$, whence $g\in T$ by genericity. Returning to the first equality we conclude that $\xi$ is the trivial character of $T$.
nodes.statement_short: The residual equality on $T_{r_0}$ gives $g\in T$, whence $\xi$ is trivial.

nodes.name: Generators of the pointwise stabilizer of a subset of an apartment
nodes.statement: Given a subset $\Omega \subseteq \apart$, the subgroup of $G$ that fixes $\Omega$ pointwise is generated by $\Zb$ (the maximal bounded subgroup of the maximal torus $Z$) and those $G_\psi$ satisfying $\psi(z) \geq 0$ for each $z\in \Omega$ \cite[\S 6.4]{BruhatTits1972}.
nodes.statement_short: The pointwise fixer of $\Omega\subseteq\apart$ is generated by $\Zb$ and the affine root groups nonnegative on $\Omega$.
assumptions: Given a subset $\Omega \subseteq \apart$
conclusions: the subgroup of $G$ that fixes $\Omega$ pointwise is generated by $\Zb$ (the maximal bounded subgroup of the maximal torus $Z$) and those $G_\psi$ satisfying $\psi(z) \geq 0$ for each $z\in \Omega$

nodes.name: geodesic $[x,y]$ and its stabilizer
nodes.statement: For $x,y\in \apart$ we write $[x,y]$ for the geodesic from $x$ to $y$; then $G_{[x,y]} = G_x\cap G_y$.

nodes.name: Setting for the generalization of Nevins' proposition
nodes.statement: The following result is a generalization of \cite[Prop 3.3]{Nevins2014}, and it allows us to relate Moy-Prasad filtration subgroups at $x$ to stabilizers of its neighbourhoods in any apartment $\apart$ containing $x$. Note that $\apart$ is the affine space under $X_*(S)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{R}$. Given two points $x,z\in \apart$, we identify $z-x$ with a vector in $X_*(S)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{R}$, and then for each $\alpha \in \Phi$, $\alpha(z-x)$ is a well-defined real number.
nodes.statement_short: In the affine space $\apart$ under $X_*(S)\otimes\mathbb{R}$, each root evaluates on differences $z-x$, which is what the next lemma uses.

nodes.name: Moy-Prasad subgroups fix simplicial neighbourhoods
nodes.statement: Let $\apart=\apart(\Stor,\ratk)$ be an apartment in $\buil(\GG,\ratk)$ containing $x$ and let $\Phi=\Phi(\GG,\Stor)$ be the corresponding root system. Let $s \geq 0$ and define $$ \Aset(x,s)=\{ z \in \apart \mid \forall \alpha \in \Phi, \alpha(z-x) \leq s\}. $$ Then $G_{x,s} \subseteq G_{\Aset(x,s)} = G_{\overline{\Aset(x,s)}}$, where $\overline{\Aset(x,s)}$ denotes the simplicial closure of $\Aset(x,s)$ in $\apart$.
nodes.statement_short: $G_{x,s}$ fixes pointwise the root-bounded neighbourhood $\Aset(x,s)$ of $x$, and its simplicial closure.
assumptions: Let $\apart=\apart(\Stor,\ratk)$ be an apartment in $\buil(\GG,\ratk)$ containing $x$ and let $\Phi=\Phi(\GG,\Stor)$ be the corresponding root system
Let $s \geq 0$ and define $$ \Aset(x,s)=\{ z \in \apart \mid \forall \alpha \in \Phi, \alpha(z-x) \leq s\}. $$
conclusions: Then $G_{x,s} \subseteq G_{\Aset(x,s)} = G_{\overline{\Aset(x,s)}}$, where $\overline{\Aset(x,s)}$ denotes the simplicial closure of $\Aset(x,s)$ in $\apart$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (Moy-Prasad subgroups fix simplicial neighbourhoods)
nodes.statement: That $G_{\Aset(x,s)} = G_{\overline{\Aset(x,s)}}$ follows from \cite[2.4.13]{BruhatTits1972}, since $G$ is semisimple and simply connected. Let $z\in \Aset(x,s)$. For each affine root $\psi$ such that $\psi(x)\geq s$, let $\alpha$ denote its gradient. Then $\psi(x)-\psi(z) = \alpha(x-z) \leq s$ so $\psi(z) \geq \psi(x)-s \geq 0$. Thus for all affine roots $\psi$, if $G_\psi \subset G_{x,s}$ then $G_\psi \subset G_{\Aset(x,s)}$. Since also $Z_s \subseteq \Zb$, we conclude $G_{x,s}\subseteq G_{\Aset(x,s)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Simplicial closure is harmless by Bruhat-Tits; then an affine-root estimate $\psi(z)\geq\psi(x)-s\geq0$ gives the inclusion.

nodes.name: Reduce to the simplicial closure
nodes.statement: That $G_{\Aset(x,s)} = G_{\overline{\Aset(x,s)}}$ follows from \cite[2.4.13]{BruhatTits1972}, since $G$ is semisimple and simply connected.
nodes.statement_short: The two fixers agree by Bruhat-Tits 2.4.13, using that $G$ is semisimple simply connected.

nodes.name: Affine root estimate on $\Aset(x,s)$
nodes.statement: Let $z\in \Aset(x,s)$. For each affine root $\psi$ such that $\psi(x)\geq s$, let $\alpha$ denote its gradient. Then $\psi(x)-\psi(z) = \alpha(x-z) \leq s$ so $\psi(z) \geq \psi(x)-s \geq 0$. Thus for all affine roots $\psi$, if $G_\psi \subset G_{x,s}$ then $G_\psi \subset G_{\Aset(x,s)}$.
nodes.statement_short: For $\psi$ with $\psi(x)\geq s$ one gets $\psi(z)\geq 0$, so $G_\psi$ fixes $\Aset(x,s)$.

nodes.name: Include the torus part and conclude
nodes.statement: Since also $Z_s \subseteq \Zb$, we conclude $G_{x,s}\subseteq G_{\Aset(x,s)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Adding $Z_s\subseteq\Zb$ to the generators gives $G_{x,s}\subseteq G_{\Aset(x,s)}$.

nodes.name: the set $\Bset(x,s)$
nodes.statement: More generally, we may define $$ \Bset(x,s) = \bigcup_{\apart \ni x} \Omega_\apart(x,s) $$ which is the union over all apartments of $\buil(G)$ containing $x$. By local compactness, this is reduced to a finite union. Let $\overline{\Bset(x,s)}$ denote its simplicial closure.
nodes.statement_short: $\Bset(x,s)$ is the (finite) union of the sets $\Omega_\apart(x,s)$ over all apartments through $x$.

nodes.name: simplicial radius
nodes.statement: Let $\Bset \subset \buil(G)$ be a bounded convex set and suppose $x\in \Bset$. For each apartment $\apart = \apart(\Stor,\ratk)$ containing $x$ define $$ r(\Bset, \apart, x) = \sup\{\alpha(z-x) \mid z \in \Bset\cap\apart, \alpha \in \Phi(\GG,\Stor)\}. $$ Then the \emph{simplicial radius} of $\Bset$ with respect to $x$ is defined to be $$ c(\Bset,x) = \sup\{r(\Bset, \apart, x) \mid x \in \apart\}. $$
nodes.statement_short: The simplicial radius of a bounded convex $\Bset$ at $x$ is the sup over apartments of the largest root value $\alpha(z-x)$.

nodes.name: Simplicial radius of $\Bset(x,s)$ and of $\overline{\{x\}}$
nodes.statement: As one motivating example, note that the simplicial radius of $\Bset(x,s)$ with respect to $x$ is $c(\Bset(x,s),x)=s$. For another, letting $\overline{\{x\}}$ denote the simplicial closure of $\{x\}$ in $\buil(G)$, we have $c(\overline{\{x\}},x)<1$ since $\overline{\{x\}}$ is constrained between adjacent affine root hyperplanes in any apartment containing $x$. Note that in each of these examples we have the equality $c(\Bset,x)=r(\Bset,\apart,x)$ for each apartment $\apart$ containing $x$.
nodes.statement_short: $c(\Bset(x,s),x)=s$ and $c(\overline{\{x\}},x)<1$; in both cases the sup is attained in every apartment.

nodes.name: Optimal points and the value $c_x$ for $\SL_n$
nodes.statement: One can be slightly more precise about $c(\overline{\{x\}},x)$ when $x$ arises as the point identified with $\buil(T)$ from a datum $\Psi$. In this case, $x$ is an \emph{optimal point} of $\buil(G)$, in the sense of \cite[\S6.1]{MoyPrasad1994}, whence the family of such values $c_x=c(\overline{\{x\}}, x)$ could be computed for any $G$. For example, if $G=\SL_n(\ratk)$, then the optimal points are among the barycentres of the facets, whence if $x$ lies in a $k$-dimensional facet $\F$ then $c_x= 1-\frac1k$.
nodes.statement_short: For a datum, $x$ is an optimal point; for $\SL_n$ these are facet barycentres and $c_x=1-\frac1k$ on a $k$-dimensional facet.

nodes.name: Mackey decomposition of $\Res_{G_y}\pi$
nodes.statement: Mackey theory gives a decomposition $$ \Res_{G_y}\pi \cong \bigoplus_{g \in G_y\backslash G/\KT}\Ind_{G_y\cap {}^g\KT}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa, $$
nodes.statement_short: Restricting the compactly induced $\pi$ to $G_y$ decomposes as a sum over $G_y\backslash G/\KT$ of induced twisted pieces.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types
assumptions: Let $y$ be a vertex of $\buil(G)$ and $G_y$ the corresponding maximal compact open subgroup of $G$.
Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ be a toral supercuspidal datum with $T=G^0$ and let $\pi = \pi(\Psi)$.
conclusions: \Res_{G_y}\pi \cong \bigoplus_{g \in G_y\backslash G/\KT}\Ind_{G_y\cap {}^g\KT}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa

nodes.name: Mackey component $\tau(g)$
nodes.statement: where each \emph{Mackey component} $\tau(g):=\Ind_{G_y\cap {}^g\KT}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa$ is a finite-dimensional representation of $G_y$. Note that since $G_y=N_G(G_y)$, the Mackey components are parametrized by a subset of the $G$-orbit of the vertex $y$ in $\buil(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\tau(g)=\Ind_{G_y\cap{}^g\KT}^{G_y}{}^g\kappa$, a finite-dimensional representation of $G_y$ indexed by the orbit of $y$.

nodes.name: Mackey components containing types
nodes.statement: If $\KT \subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$ then $(G_y,\tau(g))$ is a type for $\pi$.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types
assumptions: If $\KT \subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$
conclusions: then $(G_y,\tau(g))$ is a type for $\pi$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition (Mackey components containing types)
nodes.statement: Consider instead the twisted Mackey component $$ {}^{g^{-1}}\tau(g) = {}^{g^{-1}}(\Ind_{G_y\cap {}^g\KT}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa) \cong \Ind_{G_{g^{-1}y}\cap \KT}^{G_{g^{-1}y}} \kappa $$ which is a representation of $G_{g^{-1}y}$. If $\KT\subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$, then ${}^{g^{-1}}\tau(g) \cong \Ind_{\KT}^{G_{g^{-1}y}}\kappa$. By the transitivity of compact induction, $\cind_{G_{g^{-1}y}}^G\tau' = \pi$, whence by Frobenius reciprocity $(G_{g^{-1}y},{}^{g^{-1}}\tau(g))$ is a type for $\pi$, and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Twist by $g^{-1}$, recognize $\Ind_{\KT}^{G_{g^{-1}y}}\kappa$, then use transitivity of compact induction and Frobenius reciprocity.

nodes.name: Pass to the twisted Mackey component
nodes.statement: Consider instead the twisted Mackey component $$ {}^{g^{-1}}\tau(g) = {}^{g^{-1}}(\Ind_{G_y\cap {}^g\KT}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa) \cong \Ind_{G_{g^{-1}y}\cap \KT}^{G_{g^{-1}y}} \kappa $$ which is a representation of $G_{g^{-1}y}$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace $\tau(g)$ by ${}^{g^{-1}}\tau(g)$, a representation of $G_{g^{-1}y}$.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types

nodes.name: Simplify under the hypothesis $\KT\subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$
nodes.statement: If $\KT\subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$, then ${}^{g^{-1}}\tau(g) \cong \Ind_{\KT}^{G_{g^{-1}y}}\kappa$.
nodes.statement_short: The intersection collapses, giving ${}^{g^{-1}}\tau(g)\cong\Ind_{\KT}^{G_{g^{-1}y}}\kappa$.

nodes.name: Conclude by transitivity and Frobenius reciprocity
nodes.statement: By the transitivity of compact induction, $\cind_{G_{g^{-1}y}}^G\tau' = \pi$, whence by Frobenius reciprocity $(G_{g^{-1}y},{}^{g^{-1}}\tau(g))$ is a type for $\pi$, and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Transitivity of compact induction plus Frobenius reciprocity make the pair a type.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types

nodes.name: Mackey components that cannot contain a type
nodes.statement: Given $y, \Psi, g$ as above, suppose that there exists a nontrivial character $\xi$ of $T$ of depth less than $r_0$ such that its inflation $\overline{\xi}$ to $\KT$ is trivial on $\KT \cap G_{g^{-1}y}$. Then no irreducible subrepresentation of the Mackey component $$ \Ind_{G_y \cap {}^g\KT}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa(\Psi) $$ is a type.
nodes.statement_short: If some nontrivial low-depth $\xi$ inflates trivially on $\KT\cap G_{g^{-1}y}$, then that Mackey component contains no type.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types
assumptions: Given $y, \Psi, g$ as above
there exists a nontrivial character $\xi$ of $T$ of depth less than $r_0$ such that its inflation $\overline{\xi}$ to $\KT$ is trivial on $\KT \cap G_{g^{-1}y}$
conclusions: Then no irreducible subrepresentation of the Mackey component $$ \Ind_{G_y \cap {}^g\KT}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa(\Psi) $$ is a type

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem (Mackey components that cannot contain a type)
nodes.statement: The twisted Mackey component ${}^{g^{-1}}\tau(g)$ depends only $\Res_{G_{g^{-1}y}\cap \KT}\kappa(\Psi)$. By Lemma~\ref{L:Murn}, $\kappa(\Psi_\xi)=\overline{\xi}\kappa(\Psi)$; by hypothesis $\Res_{G_{g^{-1}y}\cap\KT}\overline{\xi}$ is trivial. Thus $\Ind_{G_y \cap {}^g\KT}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa(\Psi)$ is a common component of both $\pi(\Psi)$ and $\pi(\Psi_\xi)$. By Proposition~\ref{P:inequiv}, $\pi(\Psi)\not\cong\pi(\Psi_\xi)$. Since these are inequivalent irreducible supercuspidal representations, they have distinct inertial support, and thus no irreducible representation of $G_y$ occurring in $\Ind_{G_y \cap {}^g\KT}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa(\Psi)$ can be a type.
nodes.statement_short: The component is common to $\pi(\Psi)$ and $\pi(\Psi_\xi)$, which are inequivalent, hence have distinct inertial support.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types

nodes.name: The component depends only on $\kappa$ restricted to the intersection
nodes.statement: The twisted Mackey component ${}^{g^{-1}}\tau(g)$ depends only $\Res_{G_{g^{-1}y}\cap \KT}\kappa(\Psi)$.
nodes.statement_short: Only $\Res_{G_{g^{-1}y}\cap\KT}\kappa(\Psi)$ matters for the twisted component.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types

nodes.name: Apply the inflation lemma
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{L:Murn}, $\kappa(\Psi_\xi)=\overline{\xi}\kappa(\Psi)$; by hypothesis $\Res_{G_{g^{-1}y}\cap\KT}\overline{\xi}$ is trivial.
nodes.statement_short: Since $\overline{\xi}$ is trivial on the intersection, $\kappa(\Psi_\xi)$ and $\kappa(\Psi)$ restrict identically.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types

nodes.name: Exhibit a common component of inequivalent representations
nodes.statement: Thus $\Ind_{G_y \cap {}^g\KT}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa(\Psi)$ is a common component of both $\pi(\Psi)$ and $\pi(\Psi_\xi)$. By Proposition~\ref{P:inequiv}, $\pi(\Psi)\not\cong\pi(\Psi_\xi)$.
nodes.statement_short: The induced component lies in both $\pi(\Psi)$ and $\pi(\Psi_\xi)$, which are inequivalent.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types

nodes.name: Conclude via distinct inertial support
nodes.statement: Since these are inequivalent irreducible supercuspidal representations, they have distinct inertial support, and thus no irreducible representation of $G_y$ occurring in $\Ind_{G_y \cap {}^g\KT}^{G_y} {}^g\kappa(\Psi)$ can be a type.
nodes.statement_short: Distinct inertial supports prevent any irreducible constituent from being a type.
nodes.section: 6 Mackey decomposition and strategies for identifying types

nodes.name: The obvious types
nodes.statement: Suppose $y$ is a vertex of the facet containing $x$. Then $(G_y,\tau(1))$ is a type.
assumptions: Suppose $y$ is a vertex of the facet containing $x$
conclusions: Then $(G_y,\tau(1))$ is a type

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (the obvious types)
nodes.statement: Let $\F$ be the facet containing $x$. We have $\KT\subseteq G_x$. Since $y \in \overline{\F}$ by hypothesis, $G_x \subseteq G_y$. This implies that $\KT\subseteq G_y$, whence the first statement by Proposition~\ref{P:type}.
nodes.statement_short: Chain the inclusions $\KT\subseteq G_x\subseteq G_y$ and apply the criterion for a Mackey component to be a type.

nodes.name: Chain the stabilizer inclusions
nodes.statement: Let $\F$ be the facet containing $x$. We have $\KT\subseteq G_x$. Since $y \in \overline{\F}$ by hypothesis, $G_x \subseteq G_y$.
nodes.statement_short: Since $y\in\overline{\F}$, the vertex stabilizer contains $G_x$, which contains $\KT$.

nodes.name: Apply the type criterion
nodes.statement: This implies that $\KT\subseteq G_y$, whence the first statement by Proposition~\ref{P:type}.
nodes.statement_short: With $\KT\subseteq G_y$ the previous proposition yields the type.

nodes.name: Mackey components cut out by the geodesic test
nodes.statement: Let $g \in G$. Suppose that there exists $z\in [x,g^{-1}y]\cap \overline{\Bset(x,s_0)}$ such that $T \not\subseteq G_z$. Then no irreducible subrepresentation of $\tau(g)$ is a type.
nodes.statement_short: If the geodesic from $x$ to $g^{-1}y$ meets $\overline{\Bset(x,s_0)}$ at a point not fixed by $T$, then $\tau(g)$ contains no type.
assumptions: Let $g \in G$
Suppose that there exists $z\in [x,g^{-1}y]\cap \overline{\Bset(x,s_0)}$ such that $T \not\subseteq G_z$
conclusions: Then no irreducible subrepresentation of $\tau(g)$ is a type

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition (geodesic test)
nodes.statement: Let $\apart$ be an apartment of $\buil(G)$ containing $x$ and $g^{-1}y$; then $\apart$ contains the geodesic $[x,g^{-1}y]$. Let $z\in [x,g^{-1}y]\cap \overline{\Aset(x,s_0)}$ as in the proposition. Since $z$ is on the line $[x,g^{-1}y]$, whose pointwise stabilizer is $G_x\cap G_{g^{-1}y}$, we have that $G_x\cap G_{g^{-1}y} \subseteq G_z$. At the same time, Lemma~\ref{L:stabilizers} implies that $G_{x,s_0}\subseteq G_{\overline{\Aset(x,s_0)}}\subseteq G_z$. Thus $$ \KT \cap G_{g^{-1}y} \subseteq TG_{x,s_0} \cap G_x \cap G_{g^{-1}y} \subseteq TG_{x,s_0}\cap G_z = (T\cap G_z)G_{x,s_0}. $$ Noting that $T_{s_0} \subseteq T\cap G_z$, we deduce that any character of $T$ that is trivial on $T\cap G_z$ has depth strictly less than $s_0$. By hypothesis $T\cap G_z \subsetneq T$; so let $\xi$ be a nontrivial character of $T$ that is trivial on $T\cap G_z$. Since its depth is less than $s_0$, its inflation $\overline{\xi}$ is trivial on $(T\cap G_z)G_{x,s_0}$. We deduce that $\xi$ satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{T:inequiv}, whence the result.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\KT\cap G_{g^{-1}y}$ inside $(T\cap G_z)G_{x,s_0}$, then produce a nontrivial low-depth $\xi$ trivial there and invoke the obstruction theorem.

nodes.name: Choose an apartment and the point $z$
nodes.statement: Let $\apart$ be an apartment of $\buil(G)$ containing $x$ and $g^{-1}y$; then $\apart$ contains the geodesic $[x,g^{-1}y]$. Let $z\in [x,g^{-1}y]\cap \overline{\Aset(x,s_0)}$ as in the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: Fix an apartment containing the geodesic and take $z$ as in the hypothesis.

nodes.name: Bound $\KT\cap G_{g^{-1}y}$ using the stabilizer lemma
nodes.statement: Since $z$ is on the line $[x,g^{-1}y]$, whose pointwise stabilizer is $G_x\cap G_{g^{-1}y}$, we have that $G_x\cap G_{g^{-1}y} \subseteq G_z$. At the same time, Lemma~\ref{L:stabilizers} implies that $G_{x,s_0}\subseteq G_{\overline{\Aset(x,s_0)}}\subseteq G_z$. Thus $$ \KT \cap G_{g^{-1}y} \subseteq TG_{x,s_0} \cap G_x \cap G_{g^{-1}y} \subseteq TG_{x,s_0}\cap G_z = (T\cap G_z)G_{x,s_0}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Combining the geodesic stabilizer with Lemma on $G_{x,s_0}$ gives $\KT\cap G_{g^{-1}y}\subseteq (T\cap G_z)G_{x,s_0}$.

nodes.name: Depth bound for characters trivial on $T\cap G_z$
nodes.statement: Noting that $T_{s_0} \subseteq T\cap G_z$, we deduce that any character of $T$ that is trivial on $T\cap G_z$ has depth strictly less than $s_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Since $T_{s_0}\subseteq T\cap G_z$, such characters have depth $<s_0$.

nodes.name: Construct $\xi$ and invoke the obstruction theorem
nodes.statement: By hypothesis $T\cap G_z \subsetneq T$; so let $\xi$ be a nontrivial character of $T$ that is trivial on $T\cap G_z$. Since its depth is less than $s_0$, its inflation $\overline{\xi}$ is trivial on $(T\cap G_z)G_{x,s_0}$. We deduce that $\xi$ satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{T:inequiv}, whence the result.
nodes.statement_short: Pick a nontrivial $\xi$ trivial on $T\cap G_z$; it satisfies the hypotheses of the obstruction theorem.

nodes.name: the fixed point set $\buil^T$ and the simplicial radius $c_T$
nodes.statement: Let $$ \buil^T = \{z\in \buil(G) \mid T\subseteq G_z\} $$ be the set of fixed points of $T$ acting on $\buil(G)$. This is a convex subset of $\buil(G)$ containing $x$, and it is compact since $T$ is an anisotropic maximal torus. Let $c_T$ denote the simplicial radius of $\buil^T$ with respect to $x$, as per Definition~\ref{Def:simplicialradius}.
nodes.statement_short: $\buil^T$ is the compact convex fixed-point set of $T$ in $\buil(G)$ and $c_T$ its simplicial radius at $x$.

nodes.name: When the geodesic test applies throughout an apartment
nodes.statement: Now let $\apart$ be an apartment containing $x$. The hypothesis of Proposition~\ref{P:line} will be satisfied for all $g^{-1}y\in \apart$ if $\apart^T=\apart \cap \buil^T$ is contained in the interior of the simplicial closure $\overline{\Aset(x,s_0)}$ of $\Aset(x,s_0)$. In particular this holds if $s_0> c_T \geq r(\buil^T,\apart,x)$.
nodes.statement_short: The geodesic test applies to all $g^{-1}y$ in $\apart$ once $s_0>c_T$.

nodes.name: Unicity of types for toral supercuspidal representations
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a tamely ramified anisotropic maximal torus of $G$ and let $s_0>c_T$. Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ be any toral supercuspidal datum such that $G^0=T$ and such that the depth of $\phi_0$ is at least $2s_0$. Then $\pi(\Psi)$ satisfies the conjecture of unicity of types relative to any maximal compact open subgroup of $G$. If moreover $\buil^T$ is the closure of a single facet of $\buil(G)$ then $\pi(\Psi)$ has the property of strong unicity.
nodes.statement_short: If $s_0>c_T$ then $\pi(\Psi)$ satisfies unicity, and strong unicity when $\buil^T$ is the closure of one facet.
assumptions: Let $T$ be a tamely ramified anisotropic maximal torus of $G$
let $s_0>c_T$
Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ be any toral supercuspidal datum such that $G^0=T$ and such that the depth of $\phi_0$ is at least $2s_0$
conclusions: Then $\pi(\Psi)$ satisfies the conjecture of unicity of types relative to any maximal compact open subgroup of $G$
If moreover $\buil^T$ is the closure of a single facet of $\buil(G)$ then $\pi(\Psi)$ has the property of strong unicity

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem (unicity of types)
nodes.statement: Let $g\in G_y\backslash G / \KT$. Suppose first that $g^{-1}y \in \buil^T$, so that $T\subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$. Since $s_0>c_T$, we have $g^{-1}y \in \Bset(x,s_0)$ so $G_{x,s_0}\subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$ as well. Thus $\KT \subseteq TG_{x,s_0} \subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$ and by the same argument as Lemma~\ref{L:obvious}, we conclude that $(G_{y},\tau(g))$ is a type for $\pi$. Now suppose that $g^{-1}y \notin \buil^T$, so that $T \not\subset G_{g^{-1}y}$. Since $s_0>c_T$, $\Bset(x,s_0)$ contains an open neighbourhood of $\buil^T$, so the line $[x,g^{-1}y]$ must meet $\Bset(x,s_0) \setminus \buil^T$ in at least one point $z$. Using now Proposition~\ref{P:line}, we conclude that the corresponding Mackey component contains no types for $\pi(\Psi)$. Finally, we note that if $\buil^T = \overline{\F}$ for a facet $\F\subset\buil(G)$, then since $G$ is semisimple simply connected, each orbit of a vertex $y$ in $\buil(G)$ meets $\buil^T$ at most once. By the above arguments, this implies strong unicity.
nodes.statement_short: Case split on whether $g^{-1}y$ lies in $\buil^T$: inside gives a type, outside the geodesic test kills the component; a single facet forces at most one orbit hit.

nodes.name: Case $g^{-1}y \in \buil^T$
nodes.statement: Let $g\in G_y\backslash G / \KT$. Suppose first that $g^{-1}y \in \buil^T$, so that $T\subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$. Since $s_0>c_T$, we have $g^{-1}y \in \Bset(x,s_0)$ so $G_{x,s_0}\subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$ as well. Thus $\KT \subseteq TG_{x,s_0} \subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$ and by the same argument as Lemma~\ref{L:obvious}, we conclude that $(G_{y},\tau(g))$ is a type for $\pi$.
nodes.statement_short: Inside the fixed-point set, $\KT\subseteq G_{g^{-1}y}$ so the component is a type.

nodes.name: Case $g^{-1}y \notin \buil^T$
nodes.statement: Now suppose that $g^{-1}y \notin \buil^T$, so that $T \not\subset G_{g^{-1}y}$. Since $s_0>c_T$, $\Bset(x,s_0)$ contains an open neighbourhood of $\buil^T$, so the line $[x,g^{-1}y]$ must meet $\Bset(x,s_0) \setminus \buil^T$ in at least one point $z$. Using now Proposition~\ref{P:line}, we conclude that the corresponding Mackey component contains no types for $\pi(\Psi)$.
nodes.statement_short: Outside, the geodesic meets $\Bset(x,s_0)\setminus\buil^T$, so the geodesic test rules out types.

nodes.name: Deduce strong unicity when $\buil^T$ is one facet closure
nodes.statement: Finally, we note that if $\buil^T = \overline{\F}$ for a facet $\F\subset\buil(G)$, then since $G$ is semisimple simply connected, each orbit of a vertex $y$ in $\buil(G)$ meets $\buil^T$ at most once. By the above arguments, this implies strong unicity.
nodes.statement_short: Each vertex orbit meets a single facet closure at most once, giving strong unicity.

nodes.name: Unramified anisotropic tori fix a single vertex
nodes.statement: By \cite[3.6.1]{Tits1979}, if $T$ is an anisotropic maximal torus which splits over an unramified extension, then $\buil^T$ consists of a single vertex, namely $\{x\}$, whence $c_T=0$.
nodes.statement_short: An unramified anisotropic maximal torus has $\buil^T=\{x\}$, so $c_T=0$.
assumptions: if $T$ is an anisotropic maximal torus which splits over an unramified extension
conclusions: then $\buil^T$ consists of a single vertex, namely $\{x\}$, whence $c_T=0$

nodes.name: Strong unicity for unramified tori
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be an \emph{unramified} anisotropic maximal torus of $G$. Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ be any toral supercuspidal datum such that $G^0=T$. Then $\pi(\Psi)$ satisfies strong unicity of types relative to any maximal compact open subgroup of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: For unramified anisotropic maximal tori, every toral supercuspidal satisfies strong unicity, with no depth hypothesis.
assumptions: Let $T$ be an \emph{unramified} anisotropic maximal torus of $G$
Let $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ be any toral supercuspidal datum such that $G^0=T$
conclusions: Then $\pi(\Psi)$ satisfies strong unicity of types relative to any maximal compact open subgroup of $G$

nodes.name: Failure of strong unicity
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a tamely ramified anisotropic maximal torus. If $\buil^T$ contains two distinct but $G$-conjugate vertices $y$ and $y'$ of alcoves whose closure contain $x$, then for any toral supercuspidal datum $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ such that $G^0=T$, the strong unicity property fails to hold for $\pi(\Psi)$, that is, there exist at least two nonisomorphic types in $\Res_{G_y}\pi(\Psi)$.
nodes.statement_short: Two distinct $G$-conjugate vertices in $\buil^T$ adjacent to $x$ force at least two nonisomorphic types on $G_y$.
nodes.section: 8 The inequivalence of unicity and strong unicity
assumptions: Let $T$ be a tamely ramified anisotropic maximal torus
If $\buil^T$ contains two distinct but $G$-conjugate vertices $y$ and $y'$ of alcoves whose closure contain $x$
conclusions: then for any toral supercuspidal datum $\Psi = (\vec{G},\vec{\phi})$ such that $G^0=T$, the strong unicity property fails to hold for $\pi(\Psi)$
there exist at least two nonisomorphic types in $\Res_{G_y}\pi(\Psi)$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (failure of strong unicity)
nodes.statement: Let $x \in \buil(T) \subseteq \buil(G)$ and set $\pi=\pi(\Psi)$. Let $y\neq y'$ be $G$-conjugate vertices of two distinct alcoves $\C, \C'$ of $\buil(G)$ such that $x \in \overline{\C}\cap \overline{\C'}$. Then for any $s_0>0$, we have that $y,y' \in \overline{\Bset(x,s_0)}$. Let $g \in G$ be such that $y'=g^{-1}y$. If both $y$ and $g^{-1}y$ lie in $\buil^T$, then by the proof of Theorem~\ref{T:unicity}, we conclude that both $(G_y,\tau(1))$ and $(G_{y},\tau(g))$ are types for $\pi$ occurring in $\Res_{G_y}\pi$. Note that although these types are induced from the $G$-conjugate types $(\KT,\kappa)$ and $({}^g\KT,{}^g\kappa)$, they are not themselves $G$-conjugate since $g\notin N_G(G_y)=G_y$. Neither are these types isomorphic, since $\pi \cong \cind_{G_y}^G\tau(1)$ implies $$ \mathbb{C}\cong\Hom_{G}(\pi,\pi) \cong \Hom_{G_y}(\tau(1),\Res_{G_y}\pi) $$ by Frobenius reciprocity.
nodes.statement_short: Both $\tau(1)$ and $\tau(g)$ are types on $G_y$; they are not $G_y$-conjugate since $g\notin G_y=N_G(G_y)$, and a Frobenius reciprocity multiplicity-one argument shows they are not isomorphic.
nodes.section: 8 The inequivalence of unicity and strong unicity

nodes.name: Set up the two conjugate vertices
nodes.statement: Let $x \in \buil(T) \subseteq \buil(G)$ and set $\pi=\pi(\Psi)$. Let $y\neq y'$ be $G$-conjugate vertices of two distinct alcoves $\C, \C'$ of $\buil(G)$ such that $x \in \overline{\C}\cap \overline{\C'}$. Then for any $s_0>0$, we have that $y,y' \in \overline{\Bset(x,s_0)}$. Let $g \in G$ be such that $y'=g^{-1}y$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $y\neq y'$ conjugate vertices of alcoves whose closures contain $x$; both lie in $\overline{\Bset(x,s_0)}$.
nodes.section: 8 The inequivalence of unicity and strong unicity

nodes.name: Both Mackey components are types
nodes.statement: If both $y$ and $g^{-1}y$ lie in $\buil^T$, then by the proof of Theorem~\ref{T:unicity}, we conclude that both $(G_y,\tau(1))$ and $(G_{y},\tau(g))$ are types for $\pi$ occurring in $\Res_{G_y}\pi$.
nodes.statement_short: By the proof of the unicity theorem, $(G_y,\tau(1))$ and $(G_y,\tau(g))$ are both types.
nodes.section: 8 The inequivalence of unicity and strong unicity

nodes.name: They are not $G$-conjugate
nodes.statement: Note that although these types are induced from the $G$-conjugate types $(\KT,\kappa)$ and $({}^g\KT,{}^g\kappa)$, they are not themselves $G$-conjugate since $g\notin N_G(G_y)=G_y$.
nodes.statement_short: Conjugacy of the inducing data does not make the induced types $G$-conjugate, as $g\notin G_y$.
nodes.section: 8 The inequivalence of unicity and strong unicity

nodes.name: They are not isomorphic
nodes.statement: Neither are these types isomorphic, since $\pi \cong \cind_{G_y}^G\tau(1)$ implies $$ \mathbb{C}\cong\Hom_{G}(\pi,\pi) \cong \Hom_{G_y}(\tau(1),\Res_{G_y}\pi) $$ by Frobenius reciprocity.
nodes.statement_short: A Frobenius reciprocity multiplicity computation shows $\tau(1)\not\cong\tau(g)$.

nodes.name: A rank-2 torus in $\Sp_4(\ratk)$ where strong unicity fails
nodes.statement_short: A product of two ramified anisotropic $\SL_2$-tori inside $\Sp_4$ fixes two adjacent alcoves, so strong unicity fails.

nodes.name: Stabilizers $G_{\C}$ and $G_{w\C}$ in matrix form
nodes.statement: G_{\C} = \bmat{\R & \R & \R & \R \\ \PP & \R & \R&\R \\ \PP &\PP & \R&\PP\\ \PP&\PP&\R&\R} \quad \text{and} \quad G_{w\C} = \bmat{\R & \PP & \R & \R \\ \R & \R & \R&\R \\ \PP &\PP & \R&\R\\ \PP&\PP&\PP&\R},

nodes.name: Exact description of $\buil^T$ in the $\Sp_4$ example
nodes.statement: In the setting of the preceding example, we can conclude slightly more. First note that if $z\in \apart$ and $T\subseteq G_z$, then for each positive long root $\alpha$, we must have $0\leq \alpha(z)\leq 1$. It follows that $\apart^T = \overline{\C}\cup\overline{w\C}$, as indicated in Figure~\ref{Fig:1}. We claim that in fact $\buil^T=\apart^T$. Since $G_x\cap G_y=G_\C$, the orbit of $y$ is parametrized by the set $G_x/G_\C \simeq \GL_2(\R)/\mathcal{I}$, where $\mathcal{I}$ denotes its Iwahori subgroup. A set of representatives is $$ \left\{\overline{a} = \bmat{1&a&&\\0&1&& \\ && 1&0\\&&-a&1}, w= \bmat{0&1&&\\-1&0&&\\&&0&1\\&&-1&0} \;\;\middle| \;\;a \in \R/\PP \right\}. $$ One can verify directly that for each $a \in \R^\times$, ${}^{\overline{a}} T\not\subseteq G_y$. Thus since the fixed point set $\buil^T$ is closed and convex but contains no vertices of chambers adjacent to $x$ outside of $\apart$, we conclude that $\buil^T=\overline{\mathcal{C}}\cup \overline{w\mathcal{C}}=\apart^T$, which is contained entirely in the standard apartment. Therefore we can compute the simplicial radius of $\buil^T$ with respect to $x$, yielding $c_T=\frac12$. We had see that $\tau(1)$ and $\tau(w)$ gave types. For $a\in \R^\times$, since the choice $z=\overline{a}^{-1}y$ satisfies the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{P:line} for any $s_0>0$, we deduce that the corresponding Mackey components $\tau(\overline{a})$ do not contain types. For the remaining Mackey components, $g^{-1}y$ is not in the closure of an alcove adjacent to $x$, and Theorem~\ref{T:unicity} implies that if $s_0>c_T=\frac12$, any corresponding toral supercuspidal representation contains exactly the two types on $G_y$ identified above.
nodes.statement_short: Here $\buil^T=\overline{\C}\cup\overline{w\C}$, so $c_T=\frac12$ and for $s_0>\frac12$ there are exactly two types on $G_y$.
nodes.section: 8 The inequivalence of unicity and strong unicity

nodes.name: Exponential growth of the number of types
nodes.statement: Example~\ref{Ex:1} generalizes immediately, to give families of supercuspidal representations for which the number of distinct types supported on a given non-special maximal compact subgroup grows exponentially with the rank of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: The construction generalizes so that the number of types on a non-special maximal compact grows exponentially in the rank.

nodes.name: Products of $\SL_2$-tori in $\Sp_{2n}(\ratk)$
nodes.statement: Let $n\geq 2$ and consider the subgroup $G' \cong \SL_2(\ratk)^n$ of $G=\Sp_{2n}(\ratk)$ generated by the root subgroups corresponding to long roots. To allow us to be explicit, let the roots of $\Sp_{2n}$ with respect to the diagonal torus $\Stor$ be the set $\Phi=\{\ep_i\pm \ep_j, \pm2\ep_i \mid 1\leq i \neq j \leq n\}$, with simple system $\Delta=\{\ep_i-\ep_{i+1}, 2\ep_n\mid 1\leq i < n\}$. With respect to the basis $\{e_1,\ldots, e_n\}$ of $X_*(\Stor)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{R}$ (whose affine space is $\apart$), dual to $\{\ep_1, \ldots, \ep_n\}$, the vertices of the fundamental alcove $\C$ are $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^i \frac12e_j$, for $0\leq i \leq n$. Let $W=W_{\GG}$ denote the Weyl group of $\GG$ relative to $\Stor$. In $\SL_2(\ratk)$, there are two conjugacy classes of unramified anisotropic tori, attached to the distinct conjugacy classes of vertices in $\buil(\SL_2,\ratk)$. There are between 2 and 4 conjugacy classes of ramified anisotropic tori, attached to the midpoint of facets; see \cite{Nevins2013}, for example. With respect to the coordinates above, the roots of each $\SL_2(\ratk)$ subgroup are $\pm 2\ep_i$, and thus up to conjugacy we can arrange that the vertices have $e_i$-coordinates in $\{0,\frac12\}$, whereas the midpoints have $e_i$-coordinate $\frac14$. Let each of $T_1,\ldots, T_n$ represent an anisotropic torus of $\SL_2(\ratk)$, ordered so that: for $1\leq i\leq m$, $T_i$ is unramified and attached to $\frac12$; for $m+1\leq i \leq m+\ell$, $T_i$ is ramified and attached to $\frac14$; and for $i>m+\ell$, $T_i$ is again unramified, but attached to $0$. Then $T=T_1\times \cdots \times T_n$ embeds as an anisotropic maximal torus of $G$, and $\{x\} = \buil(T)\subseteq \buil(G)$ has coordinates $$ x = \sum_{j=1}^m \frac12e_j + \sum_{j=m+1}^{m+\ell} \frac14e_j. $$ This is the midpoint of the $1$-dimensional facet $\F$ whose closure is the geodesic $[v_m, v_{m+\ell}]$. Let $\Omega = \{\sum_{j=1}^m \frac12e_j + \sum_{j=m+1}^{m+\ell} a_je_j \mid 0\leq a_j \leq \frac12\}$; then $\F \subseteq \Omega$ and one can verify directly that $\Omega = \{z \in \apart \mid T\subseteq G_z\}=\apart^T$ using the argument of Remark~\ref{R:ex}. Note that since every maximal facet of $\Omega$ has $x$ in its closure, $\Omega \subseteq \overline{\Aset(x,s)}$ for any $s>0$. Note that $\overline{\F} \neq \Omega$ if and only if $\ell>1$. In this case, let $W^\Omega = \{ w\in W\mid w\Omega \subseteq \Omega\}$ and let $W_{\Omega} = \{ w\in W\mid \forall z\in \Omega, wz=z \}$. The elements of $W(T) := W^\Omega/W_{\Omega}$ permute the vertices of $\Omega$. Let $\GG' = \Sp_{2m}\times \SL_2^\ell \times \Sp_{2n-2m-2\ell}\subseteq \GG$; then we can identify $W(T)$ with $W_\GG/W_{\GG'}$. The vertices of $\Omega\cap \C$ are $v_{m}, \ldots, v_{m+\ell}$. The vertices $v_m$ and $v_{m+\ell}$ are fixed by each element of $W(T)$, but the orbit of $y=v_{m+t}$ under $W(T)$, for $0<t<\ell$, contains $\left(\begin{smallmatrix} \ell\\ t\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ distinct vertices of $\Omega$. Let $\Psi$ be any toral supercuspidal datum such that $G^0=T$, and $\pi=\pi(\Psi)$. By the argument of the proof of Lemma~\ref{L:strongunicityfails}, for each vertex $y=v_{m+t}$ with $0<t<\ell$, $\Res_{G_y}\pi$ contains $\left(\begin{smallmatrix} \ell\\ t\end{smallmatrix}\right)>1$ inequivalent types.
nodes.statement_short: For $T=T_1\times\cdots\times T_n$ in $\Sp_{2n}$, the vertex $v_{m+t}$ carries $\binom{\ell}{t}$ inequivalent types.

nodes.name: Broader families of tori
nodes.statement: The quadratic tori of Examples~\ref{Ex:1} and \ref{Ex:2} are the smallest of a broad class of tori to which the preceding arguments apply. For example, using L.~Morris's classification of anisotropic maximal principal tori of $\Sp_{2n}(\ratk)$ in \cite{Morris1991} one can explicitly construct products of tori of arbitrary rank, obtaining analogous results. Similar constructive arguments may be made for groups of type $B_n$ and $D_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Morris's classification of anisotropic principal tori of $\Sp_{2n}$ yields analogous examples, also in types $B_n$ and $D_n$.

nodes.name: Determining the fixed points of an anisotropic maximal torus
nodes.statement: The question of determining the fixed points of an anisotropic maximal torus $T$ acting on $\buil(G)$ was partially addressed by F.~Hurst in his thesis \cite{Hurstthesis}.
nodes.statement_short: Determining $\buil^T$ in general is only partially resolved.

nodes.name: Hurst's characterization of Coxeter tori
nodes.statement: Under the hypotheses that $\GG$ is simple, connected and split over $\ratk$ (but not of type $E_7$ or $E_8$), that $T$ splits over a purely tamely ramified cyclic Galois extension, and some mild assumptions on $\ratk$, Hurst proves that $\buil^{T_{0+}} = \overline{\{x\}}$ if and only if $T$ is a Coxeter torus (in which case $x$ lies in an alcove) \cite[Satz 13.14]{Hurstthesis}. For other $T$, he shows that $x$ lies on the wall of an alcove. Then it follows that $\buil^{T_{0+}}$ contains the closure of the $G_x$-orbit of this alcove in $\buil(G)$, since $T_{0+}\subseteq G_{x,0+} \subseteq G_{\C}$ for all alcoves $\C$ adjacent to $x$. (This is deduced via more explicit arguments in \cite[Satz 13.15]{Hurstthesis}.)
nodes.statement_short: Under Hurst's hypotheses, $\buil^{T_{0+}}=\overline{\{x\}}$ exactly for Coxeter tori; otherwise $x$ lies on an alcove wall.

nodes.name: An $F_4$ example worth exploring
nodes.statement: F.~Hurst computes a range of examples in \cite[\S13]{Hurstthesis}, including of particular interest one in type $F_4$ (labeled $6_p6_p$) where $T_{0+}$ fixes pointwise an alcove that is \emph{not} adjacent to $x$. Hence, this example may yield a torus $T$ with a more interesting set of fixed points $\buil^T$, and consequently be an unusual example to explore.
nodes.statement_short: Hurst's type-$F_4$ example $6_p6_p$, where $T_{0+}$ fixes a non-adjacent alcove, may give an unusual $\buil^T$.
